passage: Sharmila, you said you might join the student march next month, so let me tell you about mine. I'm Mahima. At sixteen, I joined a march for a cause I cared about. The organiser put us school kids in the front row "for the cameras". There was no water, no marshals, and no plan for what to do if things got rough. When the crowd surged, my knees went weak. I remembered that I could leave. I took two friends by the arm and slipped down a side street. The organiser never looked for us. Later I learned that people who lead well look after the young ones first.

qa.q: Where did the organiser put the school students?
qa.a: The organiser put the school students in the front row.

qa.q: What did Mahima feel when the crowd surged, and what did Mahima remember?
qa.a: Mahima felt frightened, with weak knees, and remembered that Mahima could leave.

qa.q: What could Sharmila look for in a real leader before joining a march?
qa.a: A plan for safety, water, marshals and an exit, and signs that the leaders protect the young.

qa.q: How did the organiser seem to see the students?
qa.a: As a crowd for the cameras rather than people to look after, since they were placed in front with no safety and nobody searched for them.

grounding: Mahima recalls an organiser using students as a front-row crowd with no safety, and leaving when it felt unsafe.

passage:
You want to know why I don't go to rallies without checking who runs them now? I'm Yamini. In Class 11, a college senior, Asif, came to our tuition centre and said they needed "young faces" for a protest about the bus fares. "Bring your school ID, it looks good on camera."

About forty of us went. When we got there, he told the school kids to stand at the very front, right at the police barricade. The college students stayed behind us. There was no water, no first-aid, nobody told us where to go if it got rough.

When the crowd started pushing, my friend got pressed against the barricade and started crying. I felt pure panic. Asif was shouting slogans from the back and didn't even look at us.

I grabbed her hand and we squeezed out through a side lane. I called my father. He came in fifteen minutes.

A real leader puts the youngest at the back and has a plan. And you're always allowed to leave.

qa.q: What did Asif ask the students to bring?
qa.a: Asif asked them to bring their school ID.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when the crowd started pushing?
qa.a: Yamini felt panicked and frightened, especially when Yamini's friend was pressed against the barricade and began crying.

qa.q: What warning signs showed the organiser was using the students?
qa.a: School students were put at the front by the barricade, there was no water, first-aid or plan, and the organiser stayed at the back.

qa.q: How might Yamini's father have felt when the call came?
qa.a: He probably felt scared and relieved at once, glad Yamini had left and called him quickly.

grounding: It shows a teen used by a protest organiser as a crowd and shield with little safety, recognising it and leaving when it felt unsafe.

passage:
Tuesday. At the coaching centre, a young man in a kurta handed out flyers for a rally about water cuts. "We need numbers. Come in uniform, the cameras love students." Vaibhav and his classmate Reena signed up. It felt important.

Thursday. At the rally, the organiser lined up every student in uniform along the front, facing the road where police vans were parked. Adults stood safely behind them. Nobody handed out water in the heat. When Reena asked where they should go if things went wrong, the organiser laughed. "Nothing will go wrong. Just stand strong."

An hour in, a scuffle started at the side. The crowd surged forward. Vaibhav's heart was pounding. He took Reena's wrist. "We're leaving." They slipped into a lane behind a tea stall and called Vaibhav's mother, who came to get them.

Saturday. Vaibhav told his class teacher what had happened. She wrote to the coaching centre that same day, asking them to stop letting organisers recruit students there.

qa.q: What did the organiser say about coming in uniform?
What was Vaibhav feeling when the crowd surged forward?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt frightened, with a pounding heart, and knew they had to get out.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav and Reena do that was wise?
qa.a: They left through a side lane as soon as it felt unsafe and called Vaibhav's mother, instead of staying because the organiser told them to stand strong.

qa.q: How does the class teacher respond, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She writes to the coaching centre the same day to stop recruitment of students, which protects others from being used the same way.

grounding: It shows teens used as a front-line crowd by a protest organiser who offers no safety, recognising it and leaving when it feels unsafe.
